needsYou.title: Your eye on the Prompt Author court: which of these sheets is the studio you want — and should MAX imagination mean one face or eight?
needsYou.productImpact: This decides what the new author writes for every roll. On your 73-word cyber-goth prompt: sent RAW, the engine gave eight different women with the framing held (your four-women result, at eight). With the author at LOW (it only added studio/framing sentences), the same: different women, the look kept, a steadier chest-up frame. With the author at MAX (your own instruction, word for word), it gave one striking woman EIGHT TIMES — same cut, same latex, same choker — because the author had stated everything and left the engine nothing to vary. Today's studio, for comparison, put your 73 words through the compiler and delivered seven of eight in the grey house tee, and put 'goth woman mid 30s' through it and delivered eight women with no goth styling at all.
needsYou.workedExample: Type 'goth woman mid 30s'. LOW author → six distinct goth women who read as their thirties, black lips, chokers, lace, clean studio (two of eight refused by the engine). MAX author → the same spiky-haired woman eight times. Raw, with no author at all → the engine refused it 17 times out of 18. Your call: is LOW the default and MAX a per-sheet choice, or should MAX be rewritten to leave hair/makeup/clothes open so it invents eight faces?
needsYou.recommendation: Build the author verbatim-first as you ruled, with LOW as the default; rewrite the MAX instruction so it names what it leaves to the engine (otherwise MAX = one face); never let the preset say 'sternum' (that one word flipped a passing prompt to eight refusals); and run #93's rewrite-and-retry on your full cyber-goth brief, which the engine refused 63 of 64 times in every form — raw included. — YOUR ANSWER (reply #8, 16:31): "B is the studio, for both the rich prompt and the thin one — build the author verbatim-first with LOW as the default. MAX as written gives one face eight times; rewrite the MAX instruction so it always leaves the face and a few axes open (casting call, not a portrait). D had the most realistic-looking humans but missed the brief — take a short realism clause from D's photographic language and test B+R against B. Build the refusal loop: log every refused and passed prompt, find trigger words, measured word→replacement pairs into the author's rewrite list, visible on the expanded prompt. Calibrate the preset's framing to my reference frame (28% head share) and lock framing, lighting and studio across every cast. Never say "sternum"." Filed: the register rebuild to this (author verbatim-first, LOW default, MAX rewritten to leave the face open), the B+R realism court (#128), the refusal-loop patrol (#129), the preset calibration to your 28% frame (#130).
